triage.name: Neonatal herpes simplex
triage.reason: Young infant with vesicular skin lesions, lethargy or seizures; a high-stakes diagnosis reached by history, exam, and HSV PCR of surface sites, blood and CSF.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: term 'Fontanelle soft' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Crackles' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Delayed capillary refill' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Occurs in newborns; no consistent sex difference
Incidence is higher after a first-episode genital HSV infection in the mother near delivery

risk_factors.text: Mother with first-episode genital herpes near the time of delivery
Vaginal delivery with active genital HSV lesions
Invasive fetal monitoring (scalp electrodes) during labor

exposures: Maternal genital herpes lesions at delivery
Maternal primary genital HSV infection in the third trimester

chief_complaints.text: My baby has blisters on the skin
My baby is sleepy and not feeding well

hpi.onset: Usually between birth and 6 weeks of age, most often in the second to fourth week of life
hpi.duration: Symptoms have been present for hours to a few days at presentation
hpi.progression: May begin with skin vesicles, poor feeding or lethargy and can progress to seizures, apnea, shock or multiorgan failure; some infants present with isolated skin, eye or mouth findings and others with encephalitis or disseminated disease
hpi.location: Skin lesions may be anywhere, including the scalp, face, trunk and extremities; central nervous system and systemic involvement affect the whole body
hpi.quality: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, seizures
hpi.severity: Variable; can be mild with only skin lesions or severe with shock and multiorgan failure
hpi.timing: Continuous or progressive over hours to days
pertinent_negatives: Symptoms beginning after 6 weeks of age
Clear watery nasal discharge with cough and wheeze

argues_against: Isolated skin lesions without neurologic signs
Isolated conjunctivitis without skin or systemic findings

atypical.how_it_differs: Some infants have only a single vesicle or no skin lesions at all, presenting with isolated encephalitis or disseminated disease; others have only eye or mouth findings.
Infants with immunodeficiency may have more extensive, atypical or chronic skin lesions and a more severe course.

general.mild: Well-appearing, alert, feeding, with only skin, eye or mouth lesions
general.moderate: Irritable or sleepy, feeding poorly, may have a temperature
general.severe: Lethargic, poorly responsive, may have seizures or respiratory pauses
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, floppy, mottled, apneic, in shock

findings.maneuver: Inspect the entire skin surface, including the scalp, palms, soles and diaper area
findings.finding: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, sometimes crusted or umbilicated

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, buccal mucosa, tongue and palate
findings.finding: Vesicles or shallow ulcers on the lips or oral mucosa

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae and eyelids
findings.finding: Conjunctival injection with watery or purulent discharge

findings.maneuver: Examine the cornea with a bright light or fluorescein if available
Palpate the anterior fontanelle with the infant upright and calm
Palpate the anterior fontanelle
Observe the infant's level of alertness and response to handling
Observe the infant's behavior and consolability
Assess tone by passive limb movement and head control
Observe for abnormal movements and ask the parents to describe any episodes
findings.finding: Focal or generalized seizures, sometimes subtle (lip smacking, eye deviation, cycling)

findings.maneuver: Gently flex the neck and assess for resistance
Observe breathing for pauses and count the respiratory rate
Auscultate the lungs and observe the work of breathing
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and count the heart rate
findings.finding: Heart rate above the normal range for age

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure with an appropriately sized cuff
Press the sternum or a fingertip and time the return of color
Inspect the skin color and perfusion
Palpate the abdomen for liver edge
Palpate the abdomen
Observe a feeding or ask the parents about feeding
findings.finding: Poor feeding or refusal to feed

labs.caveat: In neonatal HSV encephalitis the CSF pleocytosis is often mononuclear-predominant and may be modest; a normal CSF cell count does not exclude the diagnosis.
Mildly low or normal; a very low CSF glucose with high protein also raises bacterial meningitis.
Bloody CSF can reflect hemorrhagic necrosis of HSV encephalitis, but often reflects a traumatic tap.
Normal or low in many infants; leukopenia and thrombocytopenia suggest disseminated disease.
Thrombocytopenia supports disseminated disease with coagulopathy.
Transaminitis is common in disseminated neonatal HSV and can mimic hepatitis.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with transaminitis suggests disseminated disease with hepatic involvement.
Elevated creatinine in a neonate reflects renal involvement or poor perfusion in disseminated disease.
Elevated with shock or multiorgan failure.
Prolonged in disseminated disease with disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Low fibrinogen with prolonged PT/aPTT and thrombocytopenia indicates disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Swab the base of a fresh vesicle; a negative surface swab does not exclude disease, and HSV-1 or HSV-2 may be found.

imaging.study: MRI brain without and with contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected CNS disease; preferred over CT for encephalitis

findings.text: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the temporal lobes, insula and frontal cortex
findings.term: Abnormal temporal lobe signal on MRI

findings.text: Restricted diffusion in involved cortex on DWI
Normal MRI early in the illness

imaging.preferred_when: Bedside screening in a critically ill infant who cannot be moved

findings.text: Usually normal or nonspecific; may show increased echogenicity or ventricular dilatation
Often normal early; may show low attenuation in temporal lobes, edema or hemorrhage in severe disease
Not preferred because of radiation and lower sensitivity than MRI
Usually normal; may show diffuse opacities in disseminated disease with pneumonitis

initial.why: Looks for leukocytosis, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia suggesting disseminated disease
Assesses hydration, renal function and electrolytes before antiviral therapy
Transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia support disseminated disease with hepatic involvement
Screens for disseminated intravascular coagulation in a sick infant
Cell count, protein and glucose; send CSF for HSV PCR, bacterial culture and enterovirus PCR
Swab the base of a fresh vesicle for HSV PCR
Bedside screen when the infant is too unstable to leave the unit

confirmatory.why: The test of choice for CNS disease; positive result confirms neonatal HSV encephalitis
Detects viremia and supports disseminated disease

confirmatory.test: Surface HSV PCR (conjunctiva, mouth, nasopharynx, rectum)
confirmatory.why: Detects mucosal shedding even without visible lesions

confirmatory.test: MRI brain without and with contrast
confirmatory.why: Shows temporal lobe and cortical involvement typical of HSV encephalitis

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory or infectious process but is nonspecific
Elevated with shock or multiorgan failure
Helps distinguish bacterial sepsis, though it can be elevated in severe viral disease
Rules out urinary tract infection in a febrile infant

not_indicated.why: Less sensitive than MRI and exposes the neonate to radiation
not_indicated.only_if: MRI is unavailable or the infant is too unstable to be moved

not_indicated.why: Not routine; only for respiratory symptoms
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected

decision_points: Start IV acyclovir immediately when neonatal HSV is suspected; do not wait for PCR results
Obtain CSF, surface swabs and blood for HSV PCR before or as soon as possible after starting acyclovir
A normal CSF cell count, protein or glucose does not exclude HSV encephalitis
Send CSF for bacterial culture and enterovirus PCR to cover alternative causes of neonatal meningitis
Repeat CSF HSV PCR if the initial test is negative but clinical suspicion remains high

differential.name: Bacterial meningitis
differential.why_considered: Neonate with fever, poor feeding, lethargy, irritability or seizures; the most important treatable alternative in this age group
differential.trigger: Any febrile or lethargic neonate, especially with a bulging fontanelle or seizures

history: Maternal group B streptococcus colonization or prolonged rupture of membranes
Onset usually in the first week of life for group B streptococcus and Listeria
No maternal genital herpes lesions at delivery
exam: Bulging fontanelle or signs of sepsis
labs: CSF neutrophil predominance with very low glucose and very high protein
Positive CSF Gram stain or culture
imaging: MRI may show leptomeningeal enhancement or hydrocephalus rather than temporal lobe involvement

differential.name: Enteroviral meningitis
differential.why_considered: Neonate with fever, irritability, poor feeding and CSF pleocytosis; a common non-bacterial cause of neonatal meningitis

exam: Often well-appearing or only mildly ill
labs: CSF mononuclear pleocytosis with normal glucose and mildly elevated protein

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: Fever or hypothermia, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea and shock can all occur without skin lesions
differential.trigger: A toxic-appearing neonate with apnea, mottling or hypotension

history: Risk factors for early-onset sepsis such as maternal fever or prolonged rupture of membranes
exam: Signs of shock with mottling and delayed capillary refill
labs: CSF and surface HSV PCR negative

differential.name: Varicella-zoster infection
differential.why_considered: Vesicular rash in a neonate can resemble herpes simplex lesions

history: Maternal chickenpox in the period around delivery
Lesions appear in crops over days
exam: Vesicles in different stages of healing, often with a centripetal distribution
labs: Varicella-zoster PCR positive from lesion swab

differential.name: Impetigo
differential.why_considered: Superficial vesicular or pustular skin lesions in an infant

history: Lesions confined to skin, infant otherwise feeding and alert
exam: Honey-colored crusts or pustules rather than grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
labs: Gram stain or culture grows Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus

differential.name: Inborn error of metabolism
differential.why_considered: Neonate with lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, seizures and acidosis can mimic disseminated infection

history: Deterioration after feeding or a period of well-being
Family history of metabolic disease or sibling death
exam: Dysmorphic features or unusual odor may be present
labs: Metabolic acidosis with elevated ammonia or lactate
Normal CSF cell count and negative HSV PCR
Abnormal newborn screening or plasma amino acids

differential.name: Neonatal seizures from other causes
differential.why_considered: Seizures in a neonate are a common presentation of HSV encephalitis but also occur with hypoxic-ischemic injury, hypoglycemia and structural brain lesions

history: No maternal herpes and no skin lesions
exam: Normal fontanelle and no systemic signs
labs: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia or normal CSF studies
imaging: MRI shows hypoxic-ischemic injury or structural abnormality rather than temporal lobe signal change

severity.mild: Skin, eye or mouth disease only: a few grouped vesicles on an otherwise well, feeding, alert infant without neurologic or systemic signs
severity.moderate: CNS disease: lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, seizures or abnormal tone with CSF pleocytosis and a positive CSF HSV PCR
severity.severe: Disseminated disease: respiratory distress, apnea, hepatitis with transaminitis, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia or shock
severity.critical: Disseminated disease with multiorgan failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, refractory shock or status epilepticus

red_flags.meaning: Suggests CNS involvement; start IV acyclovir immediately and obtain CSF HSV PCR

red_flags.finding: Lethargy or poor feeding in a neonate with a vesicular rash
red_flags.meaning: Suggests progression beyond isolated skin disease to CNS or disseminated disease

red_flags.finding: Apnea, mottling or delayed capillary refill
red_flags.meaning: Suggests shock or disseminated disease; needs ICU-level care
Suggests disseminated disease with hepatic and hematologic involvement
Suggests raised intracranial pressure from encephalitis or cerebral edema

complications.name: Encephalitis with seizures
clues: CSF pleocytosis with positive CSF HSV PCR
Temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity on MRI

complications.name: Long-term neurodevelopmental impairment
clues: Developmental delay, cerebral palsy or epilepsy on follow-up

complications.name: Ocular sequelae such as keratitis or chorioretinitis
clues: Abnormal red reflex or ophthalmologic findings

special_populations.differences: All cases occur in neonates and young infants; preterm and low-birth-weight infants have a higher risk and a more severe course.
Infants with immunodeficiency may have more extensive or atypical skin lesions and a more severe, prolonged course.
Maternal first-episode genital HSV infection near delivery is the strongest risk factor; prevention focuses on maternal antiviral suppression and mode of delivery.

key_questions.question: When did the symptoms start, and how old is the baby now?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset between birth and 6 weeks, most often in the second to fourth week of life

key_questions.question: Did the baby have any blisters or sores on the skin, mouth or eyes, and when did they appear?
key_questions.looking_for: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, sometimes the first sign before neurologic or systemic illness

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any seizures, unusual movements, or episodes of staring, lip smacking or eye deviation?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures or subtle abnormal movements suggesting CNS involvement

key_questions.question: How is the baby feeding and how alert is the baby compared with usual?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, lethargy or irritability suggesting progression beyond isolated skin disease

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any pauses in breathing, vomiting, or episodes of turning blue?
key_questions.looking_for: Apnea, vomiting or cyanotic spells suggesting severe or disseminated disease

key_questions.question: Has the baby had a fever or felt cold to the touch?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever or hypothermia; temperature instability is common in neonatal infection

key_questions.question: Did the mother have any history of genital herpes, and did she have sores or blisters around the time of delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal genital HSV lesions at delivery, especially a first-episode infection near term

key_questions.question: Was this the mother's first episode of genital herpes, or has she had it before?
key_questions.looking_for: First-episode genital HSV near delivery carries the highest risk of transmission

key_questions.question: How was the baby delivered, and how long was the time between rupture of membranes and delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Vaginal delivery with active lesions, or prolonged rupture of membranes

key_questions.question: Were internal monitors such as a scalp electrode used during labor?
key_questions.looking_for: Invasive fetal monitoring, which can introduce virus through breaks in the skin

key_questions.question: Was the baby born early or at a low birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity or low birth weight, which increase risk and severity

key_questions.question: Does the mother have HIV or any condition or medication that weakens the immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal immunosuppression, a weaker risk factor

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any sick contacts with cold sores, chickenpox or other rashes?
key_questions.looking_for: Postnatal exposure to HSV or varicella from caregivers or siblings

reasoning_points: A neonate or young infant with grouped vesicular skin lesions, poor feeding, lethargy or seizures
Onset between birth and 6 weeks of age, most often in the second to fourth week of life
Maternal first-episode genital herpes near delivery, active genital lesions at delivery, prolonged rupture of membranes or invasive fetal monitoring
Three recognized patterns: skin-eye-mouth disease, CNS disease with encephalitis, and disseminated disease with hepatitis, coagulopathy or shock
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein and a positive CSF HSV PCR confirms CNS disease
HSV PCR from the base of a fresh vesicle, blood and surface sites supports the diagnosis
MRI brain showing temporal lobe or cortical T2 hyperintensity supports HSV encephalitis
Bacterial meningitis, enteroviral meningitis, neonatal sepsis, varicella and impetigo are the main alternatives to exclude
IV acyclovir must be started immediately on suspicion, without waiting for PCR results

easy: Neonate in the second to fourth week of life with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Mother with a history of genital herpes or active lesions at delivery
Poor feeding, lethargy and irritability accompanying the rash
CSF pleocytosis with a positive CSF HSV PCR
medium: Infant with seizures and lethargy but no skin lesions (CNS disease without skin involvement)
Infant with fever, poor feeding and transaminitis suggesting disseminated disease
Normal CSF cell count and protein despite HSV encephalitis
Vesicles limited to the eye or mouth without systemic signs
hard: Well-appearing infant with a single vesicle and no other findings
Preterm infant with apnea and shock where bacterial sepsis is the leading concern
Infant with a vesicular rash resembling varicella or impetigo
Initial CSF HSV PCR negative but clinical suspicion remains high, requiring repeat testing
Infant with lethargy, vomiting and acidosis mimicking an inborn error of metabolism
